PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN) -- Cambodia has sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council to call attention to its continuing standoff with Thailand over an ancient border temple on disputed land. Cambodian soldiers stand guard near Preah Vihear temple, close to the Thai border. The country is not asking for U.N. intervention, said Information Minister Kheu Kanharith. Rather, the letter that Cambodia's permanent mission in New York submitted to the chairmen of the Security Council and the General Assembly is meant to draw attention to a crisis that entered its sixth day Sunday. The two countries agreed to meet Monday to defuse tensions -- even as each side continued to amass more troops to the site of the Preah Vihear temple. Both Cambodia and Thailand lay claim to the 11th century temple, which sits atop a cliff on Cambodian soil but has its most accessible entrance on the Thai side. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand claims, however, that the 1.8 square mile (4.6 sq. km) area around it was never fully demarcated. Thailand further says that the dispute arose from the fact that the Cambodian government used a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia that places both the temple and the surrounding area in that country's territory. Earlier this month, the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to have the temple listed as a World Heritage Site -- places the U.N. says have outstanding universal value. The decision re-ignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it difficult for their country to lay claim to disputed land around the temple. Opposition parties in Thailand used the issue to attack the government, which initially backed the heritage listing. A Thai court overturned the pact, prompting the resignation of Thailand's foreign minister, Noppadon Pattama. He had endorsed the application. Cambodia, meanwhile, is preparing for general elections on July 27. And Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since the mid-1980s, has portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph. The current flare-up began Tuesday, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who crossed into the area. Once they were let go, the three refused to leave the territory. Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually built up their numbers. Thailand denies the charge, saying its troops are deployed in Thai territory. Each side has asked its troops to withhold fire unless they are fired upon. So far, the only casualty has been a Thai soldier who was injured Tuesday by a landmine -- possibly left over from the time the Khmer Rouge occupied the area. The Khmer Rouge, a radical communist movement that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979, won power through a guerrilla war. It is remembered for the deaths of as many as 1.5 million Cambodians. -- Journalist Soeum Yin contributed to this report .

Cambodian soldiers are standing guard near Preah Vihear temple, close to the Thai border.

Information Minister Kheu Kanharith said Cambodia is not seeking U.N. intervention. Rather, the letter, submitted by Cambodia’s permanent mission in New York to the chairmen of the Security Council and the General Assembly, is intended to highlight a crisis that entered its sixth day on Sunday.

The two countries agreed to meet Monday in an effort to defuse tensions, even as both sides continued to send additional troops to the area around Preah Vihear temple.

The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand, however, maintains that the 1.8-square-mile (4.6-square-kilometer) area surrounding it was never fully demarcated.

Thailand further contends that the dispute stems from the Cambodian government’s use of a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia, which places both the temple and the surrounding area within Cambodian territory.

Earlier this month, the United Nations approved Cambodia’s application to list the temple as a World Heritage Site — a designation for places the U.N. says have outstanding universal value. The decision reignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it more difficult for their country to claim the disputed land around the temple.

Opposition parties in Thailand seized on the issue to attack the government, which had initially supported the heritage listing. A Thai court later overturned the pact, prompting the resignation of Thailand’s foreign minister, Noppadon Pattama, who had endorsed the application.

Cambodia, meanwhile, is preparing for general elections on July 27. Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since the mid-1980s, has portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph.

The current flare-up began Tuesday, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who had crossed into the area. After they were released, the three refused to leave the territory.

Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually increased their numbers. Thailand denies the allegation, saying its troops are deployed on Thai territory.

Both sides have instructed their troops to withhold fire unless fired upon. So far, the only casualty has been a Thai soldier injured Tuesday by a landmine, possibly left over from the period when the Khmer Rouge occupied the area.

The Khmer Rouge, a radical communist movement that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979, came to power through a guerrilla war. It is remembered for the deaths of as many as 1.5 million Cambodians.

Thailand also says the disagreement stems from Cambodia’s use of a map produced during the French colonial period, which shows both the temple and nearby land as part of Cambodia.

Earlier this month, the United Nations accepted Cambodia’s request to designate the temple as a World Heritage Site, a status given to places the U.N. describes as having exceptional universal significance. That move revived tensions, as some Thais worried it could weaken Thailand’s ability to claim the contested land around the temple.

In Thailand, opposition groups seized on the dispute to criticize the government, which had at first supported the heritage listing. A Thai court later struck down the agreement, leading Foreign Minister Noppadon Pattama to resign. He had approved the application.

Both countries have instructed their soldiers not to shoot unless they come under fire first. To date, the only reported casualty has been a Thai soldier wounded Tuesday by a landmine, possibly dating from the period when the Khmer Rouge controlled the area.

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — Tensions between Cambodia and Thailand have risen sharply along their disputed border near the ancient Preah Vihear temple, as both sides reinforce military positions following a diplomatic confrontation over the site’s listing as a UNESCO World Heritage landmark.

Cambodian officials in Phnom Penh said the deployment of Thai troops near the temple area amounted to a violation of Cambodian sovereignty, while Thai authorities insisted their forces were operating within territory they consider disputed. The standoff has revived one of Southeast Asia’s most sensitive border disputes, rooted in colonial-era maps, nationalist politics and competing claims over land surrounding the 11th-century Hindu temple.

Preah Vihear, perched on a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, has long been a symbol of Cambodian heritage. In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that the temple itself belonged to Cambodia, a decision Thailand accepted at the time but later challenged in practice over the surrounding border area. The land adjacent to the temple, particularly a roughly 4.6-square-kilometer zone, remains contested.

The latest escalation followed Cambodia’s successful bid to have Preah Vihear inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. While Cambodia celebrated the designation as international recognition of its cultural patrimony, the move triggered an angry backlash in Thailand, where critics accused the government of conceding too much to Phnom Penh. Thai nationalists argued that the listing could prejudice future negotiations over the disputed territory.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen’s government has portrayed the UNESCO decision as a diplomatic victory and a matter of national pride. Officials have accused Thailand of allowing domestic political pressure to spill across the border.

“This temple is Cambodian, legally and historically,” a Cambodian government spokesman said in Phnom Penh. “We do not seek confrontation, but we will defend our sovereignty.”

Thai officials have called for negotiations and urged Cambodia not to internationalize the dispute, while maintaining that the border around the temple has not been fully demarcated. Bangkok has also faced pressure from opposition groups and nationalist activists who say Thailand must not surrender claims to territory near the site.

Reports from the border indicate that troops from both countries have taken up positions near Preah Vihear, raising fears of a clash. Cambodian military commanders said their forces were on alert but had been instructed to avoid firing unless attacked. Thai commanders issued similar statements, saying their troops were exercising restraint.

The military buildup has alarmed residents in villages near the frontier, some of whom have begun moving away from the area amid uncertainty over whether the standoff will worsen. Local authorities on the Cambodian side said they were preparing emergency measures in case fighting breaks out.

Diplomats in Phnom Penh and Bangkok have urged restraint, warning that armed conflict would damage relations between the two neighbors and threaten regional stability. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has traditionally avoided direct intervention in bilateral disputes, but the confrontation has tested the bloc’s preference for quiet diplomacy.

At the heart of the crisis is a complex mix of law, history and politics. The 1962 International Court of Justice ruling awarded the temple to Cambodia based largely on a French colonial-era map. Thailand has long argued that the court decision did not settle ownership of the surrounding land, leaving room for competing claims. Cambodia maintains that the ruling, combined with subsequent legal and diplomatic recognition, confirms its rights over the temple and its immediate vicinity.

UNESCO’s role has further complicated matters. The World Heritage designation applies to the temple as a cultural monument, but Thailand’s critics fear that international recognition of Cambodia’s management plan could strengthen Phnom Penh’s position in the broader border dispute. UNESCO has said World Heritage status is intended to protect cultural heritage and does not determine sovereignty over disputed territory.

Analysts say domestic politics in both countries has intensified the confrontation. In Cambodia, Preah Vihear is a powerful national symbol and a reminder of the country’s ancient Khmer civilization. In Thailand, the issue has been seized upon by nationalist movements and political opponents, making compromise more difficult for any government in Bangkok.

Despite the troop buildup, both governments have continued to signal that they prefer a negotiated solution. Border committees and foreign ministry officials have discussed possible talks, including renewed efforts to demarcate the frontier and reduce military tensions.

For now, however, the situation remains fragile. Soldiers from both countries are stationed in close proximity, and even a small misunderstanding could spark a firefight.

As Cambodia celebrates Preah Vihear’s World Heritage status, the temple has once again become more than an archaeological treasure. It is a flashpoint — one where history, nationalism and unresolved borders converge on a narrow ridge high above the plains.

Analysts say domestic politics in both countries can quickly inflame the issue, especially when nationalist groups accuse leaders of surrendering territory. “This is not only a border dispute; it is a sovereignty issue tied to history, identity and national legitimacy,” said one regional security analyst. “That makes compromise difficult, even when both governments want to avoid conflict.”

Cambodia has called for talks through existing bilateral mechanisms and said it may seek support from regional partners if tensions continue. Thailand said it remains committed to dialogue but insisted it would defend its territorial integrity.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, of which both countries are members, has historically urged restraint in similar disputes, though the bloc’s consensus-based approach limits its ability to intervene unless both parties agree.

**Cambodia-Thailand Standoff at Preah Vihear Temple Revives Decades-Old Border Dispute**

*PREAH VIHEAR PROVINCE, Cambodia / SISAKET PROVINCE, Thailand — 2008*

A long-simmering border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand erupted into a tense military standoff in 2008 around the ancient Preah Vihear temple, a clifftop Hindu sanctuary whose ownership was settled by the International Court of Justice more than four decades earlier but whose surrounding land remained bitterly contested.

The confrontation, which began in July 2008, saw hundreds of Cambodian and Thai troops deployed near the 11th-century temple, raising fears that a localized dispute could spiral into armed conflict between the Southeast Asian neighbors. The standoff unfolded just days after UNESCO approved Cambodia’s bid to list Preah Vihear as a World Heritage Site, a decision that inflamed nationalist sentiment in Thailand and intensified domestic political pressure on Bangkok’s government.

### Ancient Temple, Modern Dispute

Preah Vihear temple sits atop a 525-meter escarpment in the Dangrek Mountains, overlooking the Cambodian plains. Built mainly during the Khmer Empire, the temple is culturally and historically associated with Cambodia, but its location along the poorly demarcated Thai-Cambodian frontier has made it a recurring flashpoint.

In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that the temple belonged to Cambodia. Thailand accepted the judgment and withdrew its forces from the temple itself, but it continued to dispute sovereignty over nearby land, especially an approximately 4.6-square-kilometer area adjacent to the site.

That unresolved boundary issue became central to the 2008 crisis. While Cambodia argued that the UNESCO listing concerned the temple, already recognized as Cambodian under international law, many in Thailand claimed the listing could undermine Thai claims to the surrounding territory.

### UNESCO Listing Sparks Backlash

The immediate trigger came when UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee approved Cambodia’s application to list Preah Vihear temple as a World Heritage Site in July 2008. Cambodia celebrated the decision as a major cultural and diplomatic victory, with Prime Minister Hun Sen’s government presenting it as recognition of Cambodia’s ancient heritage and sovereignty.

In Thailand, however, the listing became a political firestorm. The Thai government of Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej had initially supported Cambodia’s nomination, but nationalist groups and opposition forces accused it of giving away Thai territory.

The controversy fed into Thailand’s already volatile domestic politics. The People’s Alliance for Democracy, a royalist-nationalist protest movement then campaigning against Samak’s government and the influence of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, seized on the Preah Vihear issue as evidence of government disloyalty and incompetence.

Thailand’s Constitutional Court later ruled that the government’s joint communiqué supporting Cambodia’s UNESCO bid required parliamentary approval. The ruling deepened the crisis and led to the resignation of Foreign Minister Noppadon Pattama, who had been closely associated with the agreement.

### Troops Move to the Border

Tensions escalated sharply in mid-July 2008 after Thai protesters entered the disputed area near the temple. Cambodian authorities detained three Thai nationals, including activists who had crossed into the area to assert Thailand’s claim. Although they were soon released, the incident prompted both sides to reinforce their positions.

Cambodia deployed troops around the temple and nearby areas, including close to the Keo Sikha Kiri Svara pagoda, located near the disputed zone. Thailand also sent soldiers to the border, saying its forces were operating on Thai territory and were there to protect sovereignty.

Within days, hundreds of troops from both countries faced each other at close range. Some soldiers reportedly took up positions only meters apart. Despite the tension, commanders on the ground generally avoided direct clashes during the early phase of the standoff, and both governments publicly stated they wanted a peaceful resolution.

Still, the military buildup generated alarm. Cambodia accused Thailand of violating Cambodian territory, while Thailand maintained that the disputed land had never been legally settled. Nationalist rhetoric rose on both sides, with media coverage and political speeches turning the temple into a symbol of sovereignty and national pride.

### Diplomacy Under Pressure

The standoff prompted urgent diplomatic contacts. Cambodian and Thai officials held talks to defuse the crisis, while both governments faced pressure from regional partners to avoid escalation. Cambodia also raised the issue internationally, arguing that Thailand’s troop presence threatened a recognized World Heritage Site.

Thailand preferred bilateral negotiations, wary of internationalizing the dispute. Cambodia, citing the 1962 ICJ decision, argued that the temple’s status was not in question and that Thailand should withdraw troops from Cambodian territory.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, traditionally cautious about intervening in members’ bilateral disputes, watched closely. The crisis tested ASEAN’s ability to manage security tensions within the region, particularly as both Cambodia and Thailand were members of the bloc.

### Domestic Politics on Both Sides

The Preah Vihear dispute became deeply entangled with internal politics in both countries.

In Cambodia, the UNESCO listing came shortly before national elections, giving Hun Sen’s ruling Cambodian People’s Party a powerful nationalist achievement to promote. The government portrayed itself as the defender of Cambodia’s territorial integrity and cultural patrimony. The temple’s listing was widely celebrated, and any perceived Thai challenge was met with strong public condemnation.

In Thailand, the issue damaged the Samak government at a time when it was already under siege from street protests and legal challenges. Critics argued that the government had mishandled the UNESCO process and failed to protect Thai interests. The dispute over Preah Vihear thus became one front in a broader struggle over power, legitimacy, and the legacy of Thaksin-linked politics.

### Fragile Calm, Lingering Risk

Although the 2008 standoff did not immediately erupt into full-scale war, it created a volatile situation along the border. Military deployments continued, and the dispute later contributed to armed clashes in subsequent years, including deadly fighting in 2011.

At the heart of the crisis was a distinction that had never been fully resolved: the ICJ had awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962, but the border around it remained disputed. UNESCO’s 2008 listing brought that ambiguity back into the spotlight, transforming a legal and cartographic disagreement into a nationalist confrontation involving soldiers, protesters, courts, and diplomats.

For Cambodia, Preah Vihear was an internationally recognized Khmer monument and a symbol of national pride. For Thailand’s nationalist movements, the surrounding land represented a test of sovereignty and resistance to perceived concessions by an embattled government.

The 2008 standoff showed how ancient heritage, colonial-era maps, international law, domestic political rivalry, and military power could converge at a remote mountaintop temple — turning Preah Vihear once again into one of Southeast Asia’s most sensitive border flashpoints.

**Cambodia alerts UN over border crisis with Thailand near Preah Vihear temple**

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN) —** Cambodia has alerted the United Nations to rising tensions along its disputed border with Thailand near the ancient Preah Vihear temple, warning that the situation could threaten regional peace if not addressed through diplomatic channels.

Cambodian officials said they had submitted a formal communication to the UN outlining what they described as heightened military activity and security concerns in the area surrounding the UNESCO World Heritage site, which has long been a flashpoint between the two Southeast Asian neighbors.

Preah Vihear temple, an 11th-century Hindu sanctuary perched on a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, was awarded to Cambodia by the International Court of Justice in 1962. But the land surrounding parts of the temple complex has remained a source of dispute, periodically triggering armed clashes and diplomatic standoffs.

Cambodia’s government said it was seeking international attention to prevent further escalation and to reaffirm the need for both sides to respect existing legal rulings and border mechanisms.

“We call for restraint, dialogue and respect for international law,” a Cambodian official said, adding that Phnom Penh remained committed to resolving the matter peacefully.

Thai authorities have not immediately commented on Cambodia’s latest appeal to the UN. In past disputes, Bangkok has maintained that border issues should be handled bilaterally and through established joint border committees.

The border area near Preah Vihear has seen repeated flare-ups over the past two decades, particularly after the temple was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008. Deadly clashes between Cambodian and Thai troops broke out in 2011, prompting international concern and intervention by regional diplomats.

Analysts say the latest move by Cambodia reflects growing concern that local tensions could become a broader diplomatic crisis if military deployments or nationalist rhetoric intensify.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has previously urged both countries to settle disputes peacefully, though ASEAN’s consensus-based approach has often limited its ability to intervene directly in bilateral conflicts.

For Cambodia, Preah Vihear is both a symbol of national heritage and sovereignty. For Thailand, sensitivities remain high over territory surrounding the temple and access routes near the border.

Cambodian officials said they would continue to inform international partners of developments while urging Thailand to avoid actions that could worsen the situation.

No major clashes have been confirmed, but residents in nearby border communities have reportedly been advised to remain alert as authorities monitor the area.
